=== APAACPReliabilityAssessment58777commentsonquestions.pdf ===
                                            PROJECT NO. 58777

    TRIENNIAL RELIABILITY                               §          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    ASSESSMENT FOR THE ERCOT                            §
    REGION UNDER §25.508                                §                            OF TEXAS




    COMMENTS OF THE ADVANCED POWER ALLIANCE AND AMERICAN CLEAN
                        POWER ASSOCIATION

        The Advanced Power Alliance and American Clean Power Association file these joint

comments in response to Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Staff’s questions

for comment filed on January 30, 2026 relating to ERCOT proposed SERVM input and CONE

assumptions.

                                       I.       INTRODUCTION

        The Advanced Power Alliance (APA) and the American Clean Power Association (ACP)

serve as the voice1 of a diverse cross-section of the world’s leading energy companies, energy

investors, energy consumers, and power generation manufacturers from across the clean power

sector that are driving high-tech innovation through the development of generation assets including

wind, solar, and energy storage, spurring massive investment in the U.S. economy, including a

cumulative investment in Texas of $151 billion to date, while creating jobs for American workers,

including more than 125,800 in Texas alone.2 Projects developed by our member companies and

investors generate more than $690.3 million state and local tax dollars for schools, services, and

infrastructure, as well multi-generational income for Texas landowners—more than $715.3 million



1
  The views and recommendations contained in this filing reflect the position of the Advanced Power Alliance in its
capacity as a trade organization representing a diverse membership. They should not be construed to represent the
unanimous views of all individual member companies.
2
  Texas Clean Energy Fact Sheet, American Clean Power Association, September 2025. https://cleanpower.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/09/Texas_clean_energy_factsheet.pdf.

                                                         1
 annually—mainly in rural Texas.3 Our members’ projects help reduce Texans’ electricity costs

and create cleaner air, water, and improved human health.

                                      II.     GENERAL COMMENTS

            APA and ACP appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the Commission’s

questions regarding the key ERCOT SERVM input assumptions proposed for use in the 2026

reliability assessment. The outcomes of this assessment will be shaped heavily by assumptions

and forecasts for 2029, and these assumptions inherently carry significant uncertainty. That

uncertainty warrants careful scrutiny, particularly because the Commission intends to rely on the

assessment’s results when considering potential market design changes aimed at improving

system reliability if the analysis indicates that ERCOT may fall short of the three‑pronged

reliability standard.

            Given the potential customer cost implications of any resulting reforms, it is essential that

the Commission evaluate not only the base case assumptions but also a broad set of scenarios

and sensitivities around the most influential variables. Comparing the base case to a range of

plausible alternative futures will allow the Commission to weigh the costs of any proposed

market design changes against the likelihood that ERCOT’s actual trajectory could differ

materially from the base case outlook. This approach will help ensure that any policy decisions

informed by the 2026 assessment appropriately reflect both the risks and the uncertainties

embedded in long‑term reliability forecasting.

            Within this context, close examination of ERCOT’s proposed assumptions is critical.

Several of the most consequential inputs, including the 2029 demand forecast, the assumed

resource mix, and the weighting of historical weather years, carry wide uncertainty bands and



3
    Ibid.

                                                      2
 can meaningfully alter the assessment’s results. When these inputs are set at the outer edge of

plausibility, they can create the appearance of a reliability shortfall, even though more balanced

assumptions would yield a different conclusion. To ensure that the probabilistic assessment

provides a sound and objective foundation for policy decisions, the Commission should require

ERCOT to evaluate a comprehensive suite of sensitivities around these key variables rather than

relying primarily on a single, assumption‑driven base case.

                 III.    RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS

   1. At the July 25, 2024 open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
      $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the
      triennial reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has
      proposed a plan for updating this CONE value.

           a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment?
              Why or why not?


       Yes, the Cost of New Entry (CONE) should be updated for the 2026 reliability standard

assessment because the $140,000/MW‑year value adopted in July 2024 no longer reflects the

cost environment ERCOT will face for resources entering service in 2029. The capital costs,

supply‑chain conditions, and technology availability that informed the 2024 planning value have

continued to shift at a pace that makes a static CONE inappropriate for evaluating market design

options emerging from the 2026 probabilistic assessment. Without an updated CONE, ERCOT

risks understating or overstating the economics of new entry, which would distort the comparison

of reliability solutions and potentially bias the selection of a preferred market design.

       Several developments since the 2024 decision underscore the need for an update. Turbine

and battery component prices remain volatile driven by global supply‑chain adjustments,

inflationary pressures, and new manufacturing capacity coming online. The supplier landscape

for thermal generation equipment is also changing, with new entrants offering refurbished or

                                                  3
 alternative turbine technologies. Companies such as FTAI Aviation and Boom Supersonic have

announced expanded production of refurbished jet engines for natural‑gas power generation but

the scalability, long‑term viability, and bankability of these options for 2029 commercial

operation require careful evaluation before they can be considered reference technologies. At the

same time, engineering, procurement, and construction costs for both thermal and storage

projects continue to fluctuate, affecting the all‑in installed cost of new resources and therefore

the appropriate CONE benchmark. These dynamics directly influence which technologies are

economically viable and how ERCOT should model the cost of new entry for reliability

planning.

       Because these cost drivers are uncertain and could shift materially over the next several

years, relying on a single point estimate would not provide a robust basis for evaluating market

design proposals. In addition to updating the CONE value using the most current cost and

supply‑chain information, the Commission should direct ERCOT to evaluate market design

options using a range of CONE sensitivities. This would allow the Commission to understand

how different design choices perform under varying cost assumptions and ensure that decisions

remain resilient to uncertainty in future resource costs.


            b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list
               of tasks proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT's January 15,
               2026 filing an acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please
               provide recommended modifications to their approach.


            If the Commission elects to consider an updated CONE value, the scope and task list

   proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT’s January 15, 2026 filing provides a

   reasonable starting point however, two refinements would materially improve the accuracy

   and relevance of the resulting estimate. First, the Commission now has access to detailed,

                                                  4
     project‑level capital cost information submitted through the Texas Energy Fund (TEF)

    application process. These data reflect current construction costs under Texas‑specific labor,

    supply‑chain, and interconnection conditions. Incorporating a task requiring Brattle to

    integrate these real‑world cost estimates, rather than relying primarily on national

    benchmarks or generic engineering assumptions, would ensure that the updated CONE value

    reflects the most recent and relevant cost environment for new thermal generation in ERCOT.

            Second, the updated study should explicitly address the issues the Commission

    identified during its review of the 2024 bottom‑up CONE estimate.4 Brattle should be

    required to document how those concerns are being incorporated into the 2026 update and to

    present the resulting methodological adjustments. Two of the most significant items raised by

    the Commission were the choice of reference technology (Frame CT versus aero‑derivative

    CT) and the need for a system‑wide cost adjustment to account for regional variation beyond

    the Houston‑centric assumptions used previously. Requiring Brattle to show how these issues

    are being resolved would improve transparency, demonstrate continuity with prior

    Commission feedback, and strengthen confidence in the updated CONE value.


    2. ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in
       this study should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP
       compliance plan described in the Commission's rulemaking in Project No. 58480.
       ERCOT acknowledges that an updated load forecast that aligns with that
       compliance plan could be ready by April or May 2026, which would push back the
       timeline of the reliability assessment by at least a month.

            a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026
               reliability assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in
               Project No. 58480, even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?




4
  PUCT Project No. 54584, Reliability Standard for the ERCOT Market, Brattle CONE Study Report and Model
(July 18, 2024).

                                                     5
         Yes, the Commission should direct ERCOT to update the load forecast used in the 2026

reliability assessment so that it aligns with the compliance plan in Project No. 58480.5 The

compliance plan incorporates the more rigorous, statutorily grounded criteria for identifying and

including large loads in the 2026 RTP-compliant load forecast, and those criteria closely track

the final rule adopted by the Commission on February 6, 2026. Because these new standards

reflect the Commission’s most current interpretation of PURA §37.0561 and establish the

framework ERCOT must use going forward, it is important that the 2026 reliability assessment

be based on the same assumptions.

        Historically, ERCOT’s legacy Long‑Term Load Forecast, including the forecast used for

the CDR, overstated expected load growth. This overstatement did not arise from HB 5066 or the

Commission’s new forecasting rules; rather, it occurred because those standards did not yet exist.

Under the pre‑HB 5066 framework, ERCOT lacked uniform, enforceable criteria for including

large loads in long‑term planning. As a result, the legacy forecast often incorporated speculative

or duplicative large‑load projects and did not consistently require key development milestones

such as demonstrated site control, financial commitment, and meaningful project readiness.

ERCOT has identified this as a major source of planning uncertainty, particularly given the

unprecedented volume of large‑load requests and the resulting cycle of re‑studies triggered by

immature or non‑viable projects.

        In response to these issues, the Legislature enacted HB 5066, and the Commission

implemented that directive through 16 TAC §25.370. The new rule defines a “large load

customer” as an entity seeking to interconnect 75 MW or more of new or additional load at a

single site, and it is expressly designed to correct the distortions in prior large‑load forecasting by


5
 Project No, 58480, Rulemaking to Establish Large Load Forecasting Criteria under PURA §37.0561, ERCOT’s
Comments Regarding Proposed 16 TAC §25.370 at 6 (October 17, 2025).

                                                    6
 requiring that only large loads with executed interconnection agreements meeting the rule’s

disclosure, site‑control, and financial‑commitment standards be included in ERCOT’s planning

and reliability forecasts. This ensures that long‑term grid planning is anchored in commercially

viable, committed load rather than speculative proposals. Continuing to rely on the pre‑HB 5066

legacy forecast, which lacked uniformity, rigorous validation, and enforceable readiness

thresholds, would inflate projected demand, mischaracterize reliability risks, and undermine the

credibility of the assessment at a time when ERCOT and the Commission are working to

stabilize planning processes strained by speculative interconnection activity.

       For these reasons, ERCOT should update the load forecast used in the 2026 reliability

assessment to align with the 2026 RTP Compliance Plan in Project No. 58480 so that the

assessment incorporates the most up‑to‑date, validated load information. The load forecast is a

critical modeling input and outdated or unvalidated forecasts could significantly distort modeling

outcomes and lead to inaccurate conclusions about whether and to what degree the bulk power

system meets the applicable reliability standard.

       The 2026 RTP‑compliant forecast is the first forecast developed under the HB 5066 and

§25.370 framework and therefore is the only forecast that reflects the Commission’s newly

adopted validation and readiness standards for large loads. The Commission should not use the

previous legacy forecast in the reliability assessment because it lacks Commission‑approved

standards for validation and readiness and would overstate demand, misrepresent reliability risks,

and weaken the credibility of the assessment’s outcomes. A short delay in the schedule to allow

ERCOT to incorporate the RTP‑compliant forecast is warranted. An assessment grounded in

accurate, validated load data is essential to producing reliable modeling outcomes and to




                                                    7
 fulfilling the Legislature’s directive to improve the integrity and transparency of ERCOT’s

resource adequacy analyses.

           b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load
              forecast used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

       The Commission should ensure that the load forecast for the 2029 simulation year

reflects the level of demand that can realistically be energized by that timeframe. This requires

accounting for the time needed for Transmission Service Providers (TSPs) to plan, permit,

procure, and construct the transmission and substation facilities required to serve large new

loads. As ERCOT and utilities nationwide continue to observe, customer-requested energization

dates frequently do not align with feasible in‑service dates for the infrastructure needed to serve

those loads. Long‑lead equipment constraints, extended engineering cost and procurement

timelines, and workforce limitations continue to slow the pace at which new demand can be

physically interconnected. To accurately assess reliability in 2029, ERCOT should incorporate

TSP-reported construction schedules and realistic development timelines for transmission and

substation upgrades associated with large‑load requests and adjust the forecast to reflect the

practical feasibility of energizing those loads within the study horizon.

       The Commission should also require ERCOT to perform sensitivities that capture

uncertainty in two variables that materially affect the 2029 load forecast including overall load-

growth uncertainty and potential changes in load shapes resulting from transmission

cost‑allocation reform. To address load-growth uncertainty, ERCOT should develop both higher

and lower‑growth sensitivities, including corresponding assumptions for interruptible load,

demand response, or other load‑flexibility resources, to quantify how these variations influence

reliability outcomes. With respect to addressing load shape uncertainty, ERCOT’s current large

flexible load (LFL) shapes reflect significant summer‑afternoon reductions in June through

                                                 8
 September driven by the existing 4CP construct. If the Commission adopts a 12‑CP,

non‑coincident peak, or usage-based methodology, the incentives for LFLs to shift consumption

will change, resulting in materially different hourly load shapes across both summer and winter

periods. ERCOT should evaluate sensitivities that reflect these potential changes so that the

reliability assessment captures the range of plausible system conditions.

       These additional considerations will help ensure that the 2029 reliability assessment

reflects both the physical constraints of transmission development and the policy‑driven

uncertainty in future load behavior.


   3. ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR)
      Report to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and
      2029. This includes resource additions and retirements.
         a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately
             capture the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional
             assumptions should be made about resource additions and retirements?

       We recommend incorporating the most current projected capacity of TEF loan program

projects, with Commission input, into the 2029 resource mix to the extent those projections differ

from the December 2025 CDR assumptions. Because the Commission has direct visibility into

construction progress, financing milestones, and schedule risks for TEF‑supported projects, it is

best positioned to provide ERCOT with an updated and more accurate estimate of incremental

TEF‑related thermal entry for the 2029 study year. ERCOT should also include any projects that

have withdrawn from the TEF loan program but have informed the Commission of their intent to

continue development without TEF support. If these projects are targeting a 2029 or earlier

commercial operation date, they should be reflected in the supply mix given the developers’

stated commitment to proceed.




                                                9
        As one of the primary drivers of reserve margins and reliability outcomes, the assumed

resource mix for 2029 warrants additional sensitivity analysis beyond the base CDR portfolio.

We recommend that ERCOT model an alternative supply portfolio that incorporates additional

queue capacity that does not currently meet Planning Guide criteria for inclusion in the CDR but

could reasonably progress to firm status over the next several years. Applying historical success

rates for generation and storage projects advancing from the interconnection queue to

commercial operation provides a reasonable and transparent method for estimating incremental

supply that may materialize by 2029. Including such a sensitivity would help capture the

uncertainty associated with future resource development and provide the Commission with a

more complete understanding of potential reliability outcomes.


   4. Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed
      using 13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026
      simulation year. For the 2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026
      magnitude value by the ratio of the 75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th
      percentile load forecast for 2026, resulting in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for
      the 2029 simulation year.
          a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the
             2026 and 2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values
             should be made?

       While we do not take a position on the specific megawatt thresholds ERCOT has

proposed for the 2026 and 2029 study years, it is essential that the Commission and ERCOT

clearly define what types of customer load shed count toward these megawatt thresholds when

determining whether the reliability standard is met. The Commission should explicitly clarify

how customer load shed is defined and counted within the probabilistic framework.

       The magnitude threshold only has meaning if it is clear which types of load interruptions

are included in the metric and which are excluded. ERCOT’s current modeling assumptions treat

large flexible loads, including data centers and a substantial share of industrial, hydrogen, and

                                                 10
 cryptocurrency facilities, as curtailable under SB 6 implementation criteria. The magnitude

criteria are derived from peak demand estimates that exclude these large loads. What remains

unclear is whether curtailment of these large loads, implemented before any rotating outages by

TSPs, would be counted as load shed for purposes of determining whether the magnitude

criterion is exceeded.

       This distinction is material. In ERCOT’s CDR reserve‑margin analysis, scenarios treating

SB 6 large load curtailment as a resource available prior to rotating outages show a significant

increase in the 2029 reserve margin, shifting from a negative reserve margin (-5.8%) to a

substantially positive one (+28.9%). This indicates a much lower likelihood of rotating outages

for customers who are not part of the large flexible load programs. If the probabilistic

simulations rely on curtailing these large loads to maintain system reliability and avoid rotating

outages for other customers, then those curtailed megawatts should not be counted toward the

13,988 MW magnitude criterion for 2026 or the 14,509 MW criterion for 2029. Counting them

would misrepresent the reliability risk faced by the broader customer base and distort the

interpretation of whether the reliability standard is met.

       To ensure the magnitude criterion is applied consistently and meaningfully, we

recommend that ERCOT and the Commission explicitly clarify that, in calculating reliability

metrics, including frequency, duration, and magnitude, only rotating load shed affecting

customers who are not part of the large flexible load programs will be counted. Curtailment of

large flexible loads implemented under SB 6 should not be treated as a load shed event for

purposes of evaluating compliance with the reliability standard. This clarification will ensure that

the magnitude thresholds reflect actual customer facing reliability outcomes rather than internal

operational actions taken to avoid broader outages.



                                                 11
    5. ERCOT proposed using the EIA' s 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923
      data to determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation
      years. This results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for
      coal in 2026 and $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.
         a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years
              reasonable? If not, what alternative sources of information should be
              considered to determine these fuels prices?

       ERCOT’s proposed natural gas and coal price assumptions for the 2026 and 2029

SERVM simulation years appear materially understated relative to current forward-market

expectations and the structural conditions shaping fuel demand in Texas. Because fuel prices

directly influence unit dispatch, scarcity pricing, storage charging and discharging behavior, and

the modeled availability of price‑responsive demand, using fuel costs that are significantly below

market expectations risks biasing the probabilistic reliability assessment toward artificially low

scarcity outcomes.

       Forward natural gas markets provide a more accurate and timely indicator of expected

fuel costs than the EIA Annual Energy Outlook reference case. Recent forward prices for 2026

indicate market expectations on the order of the mid-$4.0/MMBtu range at relevant Texas hubs,

which is meaningfully higher than ERCOT’s proposed $2.84/MMBtu for 2026 and

$3.16/MMBtu for 2029. Structural drivers including continued growth in LNG export capacity,

rising ERCOT peak load, and increased reliance on gas‑fired generation to support renewable

integration reinforce the likelihood of higher natural gas prices than those reflected in the AEO

reference case. Coal price assumptions also appear low relative to recent delivered‑fuel cost

trends and tightening domestic coal supply conditions, though coal’s declining share in ERCOT

moderates the overall impact.

       Given these factors, we recommend that ERCOT replace the proposed natural gas and

coal costs with forward‑market data from a recent liquid settlement date and use representative

                                                 12
 trading hubs based on generator geography to derive the forward curves used in the probabilistic

assessment so that fuel inputs better reflect market expectations for the study years.

       For coal, more representative sources include recent utility procurement data, coal

forward indices where available, and updated delivered‑fuel cost information from regional

suppliers. Replacing the proposed AEO‑based assumptions with forward‑market prices would

improve the accuracy of modeled dispatch costs, scarcity conditions, and storage behavior,

thereby strengthening the reliability of the probabilistic assessment.

       We also recommend that ERCOT incorporate weather-year daily gas-price modeling to

better capture the volatility observed during extreme weather events. ERCOT proposes to use the

monthly average shape of Henry Hub in recent history to derive monthly gas prices from the

EIA-projected annual gas prices. This does not reflect gas-price correlation with extreme weather

on a daily basis. Generating historical daily-to-monthly gas-price ratios for past weather years

and incorporating these shapes into the SERVM gas-price inputs will better capture the thermal

supply curve during these events and improve the accuracy of reliability risk metrics.


           b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

       Yes, fuel‑price sensitivities should be included in the reliability assessment because fuel

costs materially influence system operations, market behavior, and outcomes. Changes in fuel

prices can shift the dispatch order, alter wholesale power prices, and affect how price-responsive

demand and energy‑storage resources participate in the market. Natural gas prices, in particular,

can become highly volatile during extreme cold, and elevated gas costs often prompt industrial

facilities, on‑site generation, and other demand‑side resources to reduce net load during periods

of system stress. Higher gas and power prices also reshape the charging and discharging

strategies of storage resources, which can meaningfully affect their availability during

                                                 13
 energy‑constrained hours. To capture this range of plausible operational outcomes, we

recommend applying +/- 20% fuel‑price sensitivities around base‑case fuel-price assumptions

derived from market forwards as it provides a reasonable and transparent way to ensure the

assessment captures how different fuel‑cost environments could materially shift system behavior

and reliability risk.


    6. For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years
       as having equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent
       years more heavily.
           a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as
              having equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT' s proposed
              weighting of weather years?
           b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional
              details on your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach
              is better than what ERCOT has proposed.


         We do not support ERCOT’s proposed weather‑year weighting methodology as it is not

yet supported by a rigorous statistical or climatological analysis that demonstrates why recent

years should receive higher weights nor does it ensure that extreme outlier years are not

inadvertently over‑emphasized. Because reliability outcomes in ERCOT are highly sensitive to

the frequency and severity of extreme cold events, any non‑uniform weighting framework should

be grounded in expert input from meteorologists and climate scientists who can assess the

forward‑looking likelihood of such events and distinguish true climate trends from statistical

noise.

         To avoid overreliance on a single modeling assumption, it would be prudent to evaluate

multiple scenarios alongside ERCOT’s proposed weighting such as a case that uses only recent

weather years with equal weighting and another that applies equal weights across the full

historical record to provide a transparent view of how different weighting choices influence



                                                14
 reliability results. Taken together, these scenarios would allow the Commission and stakeholders

to understand the sensitivity of outcomes to this modeling input and would help ensure that any

eventual weather‑year weighting methodology is statistically defensible, expert‑informed, and

appropriately balances climate trends with outlier control.


   7. ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling
      capability in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would
      account for transmission constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT
      states that any results from this analysis would be informational and not used to
      determine compliance with the reliability standard.
          a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the
              zonal level, understanding that these results would be purely informational
              and not used to determine compliance with the reliability standard?

       The Commission should not approve zonal‑level reliability metrics at this stage because

ERCOT’s current zonal modeling framework is not sufficiently developed to produce results that

are stable, interpretable, or suitable even for informational use. ERCOT’s own documentation

indicates that the preliminary zonal representation requires substantial refinement, with early test

runs producing results that diverge sharply from the single‑zone “copper sheet” model including

materially higher loss‑of‑load expectations due to limitations in how emergency transfers and

transmission constraints are currently modeled. ERCOT has also stated that the zonal

methodology is not yet ready to support reliability conclusions, which means any zonal metrics

produced now would be highly sensitive to modeling assumptions and at risk of being

misinterpreted by stakeholders as indicative of real reliability deficiencies or as justification for

market design changes, despite ERCOT’s intent that they be informational only.

           b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has
              recommended?

       A more constructive use of modeling resources would be to focus on sensitivity scenarios

for variables that meaningfully influence probabilistic reliability outcomes such as fuel prices,

                                                  15
 weather‑year selection, demand response behavior, and storage operations so that the

Commission and the public receive robust, decision‑relevant insights into the drivers of

reliability risk. Once ERCOT has completed the necessary methodological development,

validated the zonal transfer modeling, and demonstrated that zonal results are stable and credible,

zonal reliability metrics could be reconsidered. Until then, introducing preliminary zonal outputs

risks adding noise rather than clarity to the Commission’s assessment of ERCOT’s ability to

meet the reliability standard.


   8. ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the
      Commission's weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to
      reduce weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT' s proposed
      approach, the rule' s effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures.
         a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85%
             effectiveness for the weatherization rule?

       ERCOT’s proposal to move away from a fixed 85% weatherization‑effectiveness

assumption is directionally appropriate because a single, static value cannot realistically capture

how weatherization measures perform across the full range of winter conditions. The earlier 85%

reduction assumption implicitly treated weatherization benefits as uniform, even though

equipment performance, fuel‑supply risks, and operational stresses vary substantially as

temperatures move deeper into the tail of the distribution. ERCOT’s updated approach better

reflects this reality by allowing weather‑related outage risk to increase under more extreme

temperatures while still recognizing the meaningful reliability improvements achieved through

compliance with 16 TAC § 25.55. This produces a more credible representation of residual

outage risk during the types of conditions that drive the majority of ERCOT’s reliability

exposure.




                                                 16
        A more refined treatment of weatherization effectiveness also aligns with how

probabilistic reliability models typically handle temperature‑dependent failure rates, where the

relationship between ambient conditions and outage probability is nonlinear. Incorporating this

nuance helps avoid overstating the benefits of weatherization during the most severe cold events,

precisely the conditions that dominate loss of load expectation and expected unserved energy

outcomes. At the same time, the updated approach preserves the ability to reflect the substantial

improvements that weatherization has delivered during moderate and moderately severe winter

conditions.

       For future assessments, the effectiveness factor should continue to evolve as ERCOT

gains additional empirical evidence from winter operations, generator performance metrics, and

post‑event analyses. As more data becomes available, ERCOT can calibrate the

temperature‑dependent outage curves to observed performance, improving the model’s accuracy

and ensuring that the weatherization‑effectiveness assumption remains grounded in real‑world

outcomes rather than static engineering judgment.



   9. ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:
        a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If
           not, what modifications do you propose?
        b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

       As stated in our answer to Question 7, we do not recommend that ERCOT pursue

multi‑area zonal modeling for informational purposes.

       For planned transmission outages, we recommend that ERCOT not model them explicitly

in the system‑level probabilistic reliability assessment for this effort. Including planned

transmission outages would substantially increase complexity and introduce additional modeling

judgment about outage timing, coordination, and mitigation, without materially improving the

                                                 17
 core question of system‑wide resource adequacy under the assumed topology. Instead, planned

transmission outages should be managed through ERCOT’s existing operational planning and

outage‑scheduling processes, and, if desired, could be explored in separate, targeted studies or

future sensitivity analyses once the primary system‑level reliability framework is fully

established and vetted.


   10. Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input
       assumptions that Staff has not specifically flagged in previous questions.

       We recommend that ERCOT provide additional clarity on two model input assumptions

that have not been explicitly addressed in previous questions.

       First, regarding Assumption ID 1.4 on Energy Storage Resource (ESR) representation,

ERCOT indicates that SERVM will manage State of Charge based on economic optimization

rather than reliability-based optimization. Because this choice can materially influence how

ESRs contribute to reliability outcomes, it is important for stakeholders to understand the

underlying assumptions that shape ESR behavior in the model. Two of the most consequential

parameters are cycling limits and round‑trip efficiency, both of which directly affect the

availability of ESR output and reserves. To ensure transparency and allow stakeholders to

interpret SERVM results accurately, we recommend that ERCOT publish its assumptions for the

ESR fleet, including the distribution of storage durations (such as 1‑hour, 2‑hour, and 4‑hour

resources), any daily or annual cycling limits applied, and the round‑trip efficiency values used.

Providing these details would help stakeholders assess whether the modeled ESR fleet reflects

realistic operational capabilities and whether additional sensitivities may be warranted.

       Second, regarding Assumption ID 6.7 on Price Responsive Demand (PRD) and the

4‑Coincident Peak (4CP) program, ERCOT states that the impacts of PRD including standalone



                                                18
 Large Flexible Loads and 4CP behavior are already embedded in the weather‑year load forecasts.

This approach appears to assume that future growth in PRD is primarily driven by the expansion

of LFLs reflected in ERCOT’s load forecast. We recommend that ERCOT also account for

additional PRD effects associated with the growth of distributed generation, particularly

natural‑gas‑fired and other thermal distributed generators that are not captured solely through

LFL behavior. ERCOT’s Annual Distributed Generation Estimate shows steady growth in

thermal DG units larger than 1 MW, with an estimated 500–600 MW in operation in 2024 and

continued growth expected through 2029. These units are generally expected to operate during

scarcity conditions to shield host loads from high prices, effectively functioning as a form of

price responsive demand. To the extent that incremental DG‑driven PRD is not explicitly

captured in ERCOT’s load forecast and recognizing the need to avoid double counting load

reductions already embedded in historical data, we recommend that ERCOT incorporate this

additional PRD capability into the resource mix used for the modeling effort.

       APA and ACP appreciate the opportunity to provide comments in this project and look

forward to working with the Commission, ERCOT, and market participants on these important

matters.

                                    II.     GENERAL COMMENTS

          APA and ACP appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the Commission's

questions regarding the key ERCOT SERVM input assumptions proposed for use in the 2026

reliability assessment. The outcomes of this assessment will be shaped heavily by assumptions

and forecasts for 2029, and these assumptions inherently carry significant uncertainty. That

uncertainty warrants careful scrutiny, particularly because the Commission intends to rely on the

assessment' s results when considering potential market design changes aimed at improving

system reliability if the analysis indicates that ERCOT may fall short of the three-pronged

reliability standard.

          Given the potential customer cost implications of any resulting reforms, it is essential that

the Commission evaluate not only the base case assumptions but also a broad set of scenarios

and sensitivities around the most influential variables. Comparing the base case to a range of

plausible alternative futures will allow the Commission to weigh the costs of any proposed

market design changes against the likelihood that ERCOT' s actual traj ectory could differ

materially from the base case outlook. This approach will help ensure that any policy decisions

informed by the 2026 assessment appropriately reflect both the risks and the uncertainties

embedded in long-term reliability forecasting.

          Within this context, close examination of ERCOT' s proposed assumptions is critical.

Several of the most consequential inputs, including the 2029 demand forecast, the assumed

resource mix, and the weighting of historical weather years, carry wide uncertainty bands and

 can meaningfully alter the assessment' s results. When these inputs are set at the outer edge of

plausibility, they can create the appearance of a reliability shortfall, even though more balanced

assumptions would yield a different conclusion. To ensure that the probabilistic assessment

provides a sound and objective foundation for policy decisions, the Commission should require

ERCOT to evaluate a comprehensive suite of sensitivities around these key variables rather than

relying primarily on a single, assumption-driven base case.

    1. At the July 25, 2024 open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
       $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the
       triennial reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has
       proposed a plan for updating this CONE value.

           a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment?
              Why or why not?


       Yes, the Cost of New Entry (CONE) should be updated for the 2026 reliability standard

assessment because the $140,000/MW-year value adopted in July 2024 no longer reflects the

cost environment ERCOT will face for resources entering service in 2029. The capital costs,

supply-chain conditions, and technology availability that informed the 2024 planning value have

continued to shift at a pace that makes a static CONE inappropriate for evaluating market design

options emerging from the 2026 probabilistic assessment. Without an updated CONE, ERCOT

risks understating or overstating the economics of new entry, which would distort the comparison

of reliability solutions and potentially bias the selection of a preferred market design.

       Several developments since the 2024 decision underscore the need for an update. Turbine

and battery component prices remain volatile driven by global supply-chain adjustments,

inflationary pressures, and new manufacturing capacity coming online. The supplier landscape

for thermal generation equipment is also changing, with new entrants offering refurbished or


                                                  3

announced expanded production of refurbished jet engines for natural-gas power generation but

the scalability, long-term viability, and bankability of these options for 2029 commercial

operation require careful evaluation before they can be considered reference technologies. At the

same time, engineering, procurement, and construction costs for both thermal and storage

proj ects continue to fluctuate, affecting the all-in installed cost of new resources and therefore

the appropriate CONE benchmark. These dynamics directly influence which technologies are

economically viable and how ERCOT should model the cost of new entry for reliability

planning.

       Because these cost drivers are uncertain and could shift materially over the next several

years, relying on a single point estimate would not provide a robust basis for evaluating market

design proposals. In addition to updating the CONE value using the most current cost and

supply-chain information, the Commission should direct ERCOT to evaluate market design

options using a range of CONF sensitivities. This would allow the Commission to understand

how different design choices perform under varying cost assumptions and ensure that decisions

remain resilient to uncertainty in future resource costs.

         Yes, the Commission should direct ERCOT to update the load forecast used in the 2026

reliability assessment so that it aligns with the compliance plan in Project No. 58480.5 The

compliance plan incorporates the more rigorous, statutorily grounded criteria for identifying and

including large loads in the 2026 RTP-compliant load forecast, and those criteria closely track

the final rule adopted by the Commission on February 6,2026. Because these new standards

reflect the Commission's most current interpretation of PURA §37.0561 and establish the

framework ERCOT must use going forward, it is important that the 2026 reliability assessment

be based on the same assumptions.

        Historically, ERCOT's legacy Long-Term Load Forecast, including the forecast used for

the CDR, overstated expected load growth. This overstatement did not arise from HB 5066 or the

Commission's new forecasting rules; rather, it occurred because those standards did not yet exist.

Under the pre-HB 5066 framework, ERCOT lacked uniform, enforceable criteria for including

large loads in long-term planning. As a result, the legacy forecast often incorporated speculative

or duplicative large-load projects and did not consistently require key development milestones

such as demonstrated site control, financial commitment, and meaningful project readiness.

ERCOT has identified this as a major source of planning uncertainty, particularly given the

unprecedented volume of large-load requests and the resulting cycle of re-studies triggered by

immature or non-viable proj ects.

        In response to these issues, the Legislature enacted HB 5066, and the Commission

implemented that directive through 16 TAC §25.370. The new rule defines a "large load

customef' as an entity seeking to interconnect 75 MW or more of new or additional load at a

single site, and it is expressly designed to correct the distortions in prior large-load forecasting by

legacy forecast, which lacked uniformity, rigorous validation, and enforceable readiness

thresholds, would inflate projected demand, mischaracterize reliability risks, and undermine the

credibility of the assessment at a time when ERCOT and the Commission are working to

stabilize planning processes strained by speculative interconnection activity.

       For these reasons, ERCOT should update the load forecast used in the 2026 reliability

accurate, validated load data is essential to producing reliable modeling outcomes and to

           b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load
              forecast used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

       The Commission should ensure that the load forecast for the 2029 simulation year

reflects the level of demand that can realistically be energized by that timeframe. This requires

accounting for the time needed for Transmission Service Providers (TSPs) to plan, permit,

procure, and construct the transmission and substation facilities required to serve large new

loads. As ERCOT and utilities nationwide continue to observe, customer-requested energization

dates frequently do not align with feasible in-service dates for the infrastructure needed to serve
those loads. Long-lead equipment constraints, extended engineering cost and procurement

timelines, and workforce limitations continue to slow the pace at which new demand can be

physically interconnected. To accurately assess reliability in 2029, ERCOT should incorporate

substation upgrades associated with large-load requests and adjust the forecast to reflect the

practical feasibility of energizing those loads within the study horizon.

       The Commission should also require ERCOT to perform sensitivities that capture

uncertainty in two variables that materially affect the 2029 load forecast including overall load-

growth uncertainty and potential changes in load shapes resulting from transmission

cost-allocation reform. To address load-growth uncertainty, ERCOT should develop both higher

and lower-growth sensitivities, including corresponding assumptions for interruptible load,

demand response, or other load-flexibility resources, to quantify how these variations influence

reliability outcomes. With respect to addressing load shape uncertainty, ERCOT's current large

flexible load (LFL) shapes reflect significant summer-afternoon reductions in June through

 September driven by the existing 4CP construct. If the Commission adopts a 12-CP,

non-coincident peak, or usage-based methodology, the incentives for LFLs to shift consumption

will change, resulting in materially different hourly load shapes across both summer and winter

periods. ERCOT should evaluate sensitivities that reflect these potential changes so that the

reliability assessment captures the range of plausible system conditions.

       These additional considerations will help ensure that the 2029 reliability assessment

reflects both the physical constraints of transmission development and the policy-driven

uncertainty in future load behavior.


   3. ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR)
      Report to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and
      2029. This includes resource additions and retirements.
         a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately
             capture the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional
               assumptions should be made about resource additions and retirements?

       We recommend incorporating the most current proj ected capacity of TEF loan program

projects, with Commission input, into the 2029 resource mix to the extent those projections differ

from the December 2025 CDR assumptions. Because the Commission has direct visibility into

construction progress, financing milestones, and schedule risks for TEF-supported projects, it is

best positioned to provide ERCOT with an updated and more accurate estimate of incremental

TEF-related thermal entry for the 2029 study year. ERCOT should also include any projects that

have withdrawn from the TEF loan program but have informed the Commission of their intent to

continue development without TEF support. If these proj ects are targeting a 2029 or earlier

commercial operation date, they should be reflected in the supply mix given the developers'

stated commitment to proceed.




                                                 9
        As one of the primary drivers of reserve margins and reliability outcomes, the assumed

resource mix for 2029 warrants additional sensitivity analysis beyond the base CDR portfolio.

We recommend that ERCOT model an alternative supply portfolio that incorporates additional

queue capacity that does not currently meet Planning Guide criteria for inclusion in the CDR but

could reasonably progress to firm status over the next several years. Applying historical success

rates for generation and storage proj ects advancing from the interconnection queue to

commercial operation provides a reasonable and transparent method for estimating incremental

supply that may materialize by 2029. Including such a sensitivity would help capture the

uncertainty associated with future resource development and provide the Commission with a

more complete understanding of potential reliability outcomes.


   4. Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed
      using 13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026
      simulation year. For the 2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026
       magnitude value by the ratio of the 75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th
       percentile load forecast for 2026, resulting in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for
       the 2029 simulation year.
           a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the
               2026 and 2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values
               should be made?

       While we do not take a position on the specific megawatt thresholds ERCOT has

proposed for the 2026 and 2029 study years, it is essential that the Commission and ERCOT

clearly define what types of customer load shed count toward these megawatt thresholds when

determining whether the reliability standard is met. The Commission should explicitly clarify

how customer load shed is defined and counted within the probabilistic framework.

       The magnitude threshold only has meaning if it is clear which types of load interruptions

are included in the metric and which are excluded. ERCOT's current modeling assumptions treat

large flexible loads, including data centers and a substantial share of industrial, hydrogen, and


                                                 10
 cryptocurrency facilities, as curtailable under SB 6 implementation criteria. The magnitude

criteria are derived from peak demand estimates that exclude these large loads. What remains

unclear is whether curtailment of these large loads, implemented before any rotating outages by

TSPs, would be counted as load shed for purposes of determining whether the magnitude

criterion is exceeded.

       This distinction is material. In ERCOT's CDR reserve-margin analysis, scenarios treating

SB 6 large load curtailment as a resource available prior to rotating outages show a significant

increase in the 2029 reserve margin, shifting from a negative reserve margin (-5.8%) to a

substantially positive one (+28.9%). This indicates a much lower likelihood of rotating outages

for customers who are not part of the large flexible load programs. If the probabilistic

simulations rely on curtailing these large loads to maintain system reliability and avoid rotating

outages for other customers, then those curtailed megawatts should not be counted toward the

13,988 MW magnitude criterion for 2026 or the 14,509 MW criterion for 2029. Counting them

would misrepresent the reliability risk faced by the broader customer base and distort the

interpretation of whether the reliability standard is met.

       To ensure the magnitude criterion is applied consistently and meaningfully, we

recommend that ERCOT and the Commission explicitly clarify that, in calculating reliability

metrics, including frequency, duration, and magnitude, only rotating load shed affecting

customers who are not part of the large flexible load programs will be counted. Curtailment of

large flexible loads implemented under SB 6 should not be treated as a load shed event for

purposes of evaluating compliance with the reliability standard. This clarification will ensure that

the magnitude thresholds reflect actual customer facing reliability outcomes rather than internal

operational actions taken to avoid broader outages.

    5. ERCOT proposed using the EIA' s 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923
       data to determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation
       years. This results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for
       coal in 2026 and $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.
          a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years
               reasonable? If not, what alternative sources of information should be
               considered to determine these fuels prices?

       ERCOT's proposed natural gas and coal price assumptions for the 2026 and 2029

SERVM simulation years appear materially understated relative to current forward-market

expectations and the structural conditions shaping fuel demand in Texas. Because fuel prices

directly influence unit dispatch, scarcity pricing, storage charging and discharging behavior, and

the modeled availability of price-responsive demand, using fuel costs that are significantly below

market expectations risks biasing the probabilistic reliability assessment toward artificially low

scarcity outcomes.

       Forward natural gas markets provide a more accurate and timely indicator of expected

fuel costs than the EIA Annual Energy Outlook reference case. Recent forward prices for 2026

indicate market expectations on the order of the mid-$4.0/MMBtu range at relevant Texas hubs,

which is meaningfully higher than ERCOT's proposed $2.84/MMBtu for 2026 and

$3.16/MMBtu for 2029. Structural drivers including continued growth in LNG export capacity,

rising ERCOT peak load, and increased reliance on gas-fired generation to support renewable

integration reinforce the likelihood of higher natural gas prices than those reflected in the AEO

reference case. Coal price assumptions also appear low relative to recent delivered-fuel cost

trends and tightening domestic coal supply conditions, though coal's declining share in ERCOT

moderates the overall impact.

       Given these factors, we recommend that ERCOT replace the proposed natural gas and

coal costs with forward-market data from a recent liquid settlement date and use representative


                                                 12
 trading hubs based on generator geography to derive the forward curves used in the probabilistic

assessment so that fuel inputs better reflect market expectations for the study years.

       For coal, more representative sources include recent utility procurement data, coal

forward indices where available, and updated delivered-fuel cost information from regional

suppliers. Replacing the proposed AEO-based assumptions with forward-market prices would

improve the accuracy of modeled dispatch costs, scarcity conditions, and storage behavior,

thereby strengthening the reliability of the probabilistic assessment.

       We also recommend that ERCOT incorporate weather-year daily gas-price modeling to

better capture the volatility observed during extreme weather events. ERCOT proposes to use the

monthly average shape of Henry Hub in recent history to derive monthly gas prices from the

EIA-projected annual gas prices. This does not reflect gas-price correlation with extreme weather

on a daily basis. Generating historical daily-to-monthly gas-price ratios for past weather years

and incorporating these shapes into the SERVM gas-price inputs will better capture the thermal

supply curve during these events and improve the accuracy of reliability risk metrics.


           b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

       Yes, fuel-price sensitivities should be included in the reliability assessment because fuel

costs materially influence system operations, market behavior, and outcomes. Changes in fuel

prices can shift the dispatch order, alter wholesale power prices, and affect how price-responsive

demand and energy-storage resources participate in the market. Natural gas prices, in particular,

can become highly volatile during extreme cold, and elevated gas costs often prompt industrial

facilities, on-site generation, and other demand-side resources to reduce net load during periods

of system stress. Higher gas and power prices also reshape the charging and discharging

strategies of storage resources, which can meaningfully affect their availability during


                                                 13
 energy-constrained hours. To capture this range of plausible operational outcomes, we

recommend applying +/- 20% fuel-price sensitivities around base-case fuel-price assumptions

derived from market forwards as it provides a reasonable and transparent way to ensure the

assessment captures how different fuel-cost environments could materially shift system behavior

and reliability risk.


    6. For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years
       as having equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent
         years more heavily.
            a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as
                having equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT' s proposed
                weighting of weather years?
            b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional
               details on your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach
               is better than what ERCOT has proposed.


         We do not support ERCOT's proposed weather-year weighting methodology as it is not

yet supported by a rigorous statistical or climatological analysis that demonstrates why recent

years should receive higher weights nor does it ensure that extreme outlier years are not

inadvertently over-emphasized. Because reliability outcomes in ERCOT are highly sensitive to

the frequency and severity of extreme cold events, any non-uniform weighting framework should

be grounded in expert input from meteorologists and climate scientists who can assess the

forward-looking likelihood of such events and distinguish true climate trends from statistical

noise.

         To avoid overreliance on a single modeling assumption, it would be prudent to evaluate

multiple scenarios alongside ERCOT's proposed weighting such as a case that uses only recent

weather years with equal weighting and another that applies equal weights across the full

historical record to provide a transparent view of how different weighting choices influence



                                                14
 reliability results. Taken together, these scenarios would allow the Commission and stakeholders

to understand the sensitivity of outcomes to this modeling input and would help ensure that any

eventual weather-year weighting methodology is statistically defensible, expert-informed, and

appropriately balances climate trends with outlier control.


    7. ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling
       capability in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would
       account for transmission constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT
       states that any results from this analysis would be informational and not used to
       determine compliance with the reliability standard.
           a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the
               zonal level, understanding that these results would be purely informational
               and not used to determine compliance with the reliability standard?

        The Commission should not approve zonal-level reliability metrics at this stage because

ERCOT's current zonal modeling framework is not sufficiently developed to produce results that

are stable, interpretable, or suitable even for informational use. ERCOT's own documentation

indicates that the preliminary zonal representation requires substantial refinement, with early test

runs producing results that diverge sharply from the single-zone "copper sheet" model including

materially higher loss-of-load expectations due to limitations in how emergency transfers and

transmission constraints are currently modeled. ERCOT has also stated that the zonal

methodology is not yet ready to support reliability conclusions, which means any zonal metrics

produced now would be highly sensitive to modeling assumptions and at risk of being

misinterpreted by stakeholders as indicative of real reliability deficiencies or as justification for

market design changes, despite ERCOT's intent that they be informational only.

           b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has
              recommended?

       A more constructive use of modeling resources would be to focus on sensitivity scenarios

for variables that meaningfully influence probabilistic reliability outcomes such as fuel prices,


                                                  15
 weather-year selection, demand response behavior, and storage operations so that the

Commission and the public receive robust, decision-relevant insights into the drivers of

reliability risk. Once ERCOT has completed the necessary methodological development,

validated the zonal transfer modeling, and demonstrated that zonal results are stable and credible,

zonal reliability metrics could be reconsidered. Until then, introducing preliminary zonal outputs

risks adding noise rather than clarity to the Commission's assessment of ERCOT's ability to

meet the reliability standard.


    8. ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the
       Commission's weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to
       reduce weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT' s proposed
       approach, the rule' s effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures.
          a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85%
              effectiveness for the weatherization rule?

       ERCOT's proposal to move away from a fixed 85% weatherization-effectiveness

assumption is directionally appropriate because a single, static value cannot realistically capture

how weatherization measures perform across the full range of winter conditions. The earlier 85%

reduction assumption implicitly treated weatherization benefits as uniform, even though

equipment performance, fuel-supply risks, and operational stresses vary substantially as

temperatures move deeper into the tail of the distribution. ERCOT's updated approach better

reflects this reality by allowing weather-related outage risk to increase under more extreme

temperatures while still recognizing the meaningful reliability improvements achieved through

compliance with 16 TAC § 25.55. This produces a more credible representation of residual

outage risk during the types of conditions that drive the majority of ERCOT's reliability

exposure.




                                                 16
        A more refined treatment of weatherization effectiveness also aligns with how

probabilistic reliability models typically handle temperature-dependent failure rates, where the

relationship between ambient conditions and outage probability is nonlinear. Incorporating this

nuance helps avoid overstating the benefits of weatherization during the most severe cold events,

precisely the conditions that dominate loss of load expectation and expected unserved energy

outcomes. At the same time, the updated approach preserves the ability to reflect the substantial

improvements that weatherization has delivered during moderate and moderately severe winter

conditions.

       For future assessments, the effectiveness factor should continue to evolve as ERCOT

gains additional empirical evidence from winter operations, generator performance metrics, and

post-event analyses. As more data becomes available, ERCOT can calibrate the

temperature-dependent outage curves to observed performance, improving the model's accuracy

and ensuring that the weatherization-effectiveness assumption remains grounded in real-world

outcomes rather than static engineering judgment.



   9. ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:
        a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If
           not, what modifications do you propose?
        b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

       As stated in our answer to Question 7, we do not recommend that ERCOT pursue

multi-area zonal modeling for informational purposes.

       For planned transmission outages, we recommend that ERCOT not model them explicitly

in the system-level probabilistic reliability assessment for this effort. Including planned

transmission outages would substantially increase complexity and introduce additional modeling

judgment about outage timing, coordination, and mitigation, without materially improving the


                                                 17
 core question of system-wide resource adequacy under the assumed topology. Instead, planned

transmission outages should be managed through ERCOT's existing operational planning and

outage-scheduling processes, and, if desired, could be explored in separate, targeted studies or

future sensitivity analyses once the primary system-level reliability framework is fully

established and vetted.


    10. Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input
       assumptions that Staff has not specifically ilagged in previous questions.

       We recommend that ERCOT provide additional clarity on two model input assumptions

that have not been explicitly addressed in previous questions.

       First, regarding Assumption ID 1.4 on Energy Storage Resource (ESR) representation,

ERCOT indicates that SERVM will manage State of Charge based on economic optimization

rather than reliability-based optimization. Because this choice can materially influence how

ESRs contribute to reliability outcomes, it is important for stakeholders to understand the

underlying assumptions that shape ESR behavior in the model. Two of the most consequential

parameters are cycling limits and round-trip efficiency, both of which directly affect the

availability of ESR output and reserves. To ensure transparency and allow stakeholders to

interpret SERVM results accurately, we recommend that ERCOT publish its assumptions for the

ESR fleet, including the distribution of storage durations (such as 1-hour, 2-hour, and 4-hour

resources), any daily or annual cycling limits applied, and the round-trip efficiency values used.

Providing these details would help stakeholders assess whether the modeled ESR fleet reflects

realistic operational capabilities and whether additional sensitivities may be warranted.

       Second, regarding Assumption ID 6.7 on Price Responsive Demand (PRI)) and the

4-Coincident Peak (4CP) program, ERCOT states that the impacts of PRD including standalone



                                                 18
 Large Flexible Loads and 4CP behavior are already embedded in the weather-year load forecasts.

This approach appears to assume that future growth in PRI) is primarily driven by the expansion

of LFLs reflected in ERCOT's load forecast. We recommend that ERCOT also account for

additional PRI effects associated with the growth of distributed generation, particularly

natural-gas-fired and other thermal distributed generators that are not captured solely through

LFL behavior. ERCOT's Annual Distributed Generation Estimate shows steady growth in

thermal DG units larger than 1 MW, with an estimated 500-600 MW in operation in 2024 and

continued growth expected through 2029. These units are generally expected to operate during

scarcity conditions to shield host loads from high prices, effectively functioning as a form of

price responsive demand. To the extent that incremental DG-driven PRD is not explicitly

captured in ERCOT's load forecast and recognizing the need to avoid double counting load

reductions already embedded in historical data, we recommend that ERCOT incorporate this

additional PRI) capability into the resource mix used for the modeling effort.

   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF THE ADVANCED POWER ALLIANCE AND
        AMERICAN CLEAN POWER ASSOCIATION COMMENTS

The 2026 ERCOT reliability assessment hinges on long-range assumptions for 2029 that carry
significant uncertainty, requiring careful scrutiny before being used to guide market design decisions.
Several key SERVM inputs including the 2029 load forecast, resource mix assumptions, and
weighting of historical weather years have wide uncertainty ranges and can materially shift reliability
outconies.
To ensure the reliability assessment provides a sound basis for policy decisions and avoids
unnecessary customer-cost exposure, the Commission should require ERCOT to evaluate a
comprehensive suite of scenarios and sensitivities around key assumptions rather than relying
primarily on a single base case to understand how plausible alternative futures could materially
change the assessment's conclusions.

The CONE value should be updated for the 2026 reliability assessment and any updated CONE value
should incorporate Texas-specific project-level cost data from the Texas Energy Fund (TEF) and
explicitly address issues raised during the Commission's review ofthe 2024 CONE estimate,
including the choice of reference technology and the need for a system-wide regional cost adjustment
beyond Houston-centric assumptions. Because future cost drivers remain uncertain, the Commission
should require ERCOT to evaluate market-design options using a range of CONE sensitivities rather
than a single point estimate, ensuring decisions remain robust across plausible cost environments.

The Commission should require ERCOT to update the load forecast used in the 2026 reliability
assessment so that it aligns with the new HB 5066/§25.370 forecasting framework, even if doing so
delays the assessment, because the RTP-compliant forecast is the only forecast grounded in validated,
commercially viable large-load data, avoids the overstatement and inconsistency embedded in
ERCOT's legacy forecast, and reflects the Commission's most current standards for load readiness,
disclosure, and interconnection viability.

For the 2029 simulation year, the Commission should ensure that ERCOT's load forecast reflects the
realistic pace at which Transmission Service Providers can construct the infrastructure needed to
energize large loads and should require sensitivities that capture uncertainty in long-term load growth
and potential changes in hourly load shapes resulting from transmission cost-allocation reform.

The December 2025 CDR portfolio alone does not fully capture the likely 2029 resource mix;
ERCOT should incorporate updated capacity projections for TEF projects, including both
TEF-supported projects and those that have withdrawn but intend to proceed independently, based on
the Commission's visibility into construction progress and commercial readiness.

Because the 2029 supply mix is a major driver of reserve margins, ERCOT should model additional
sensitivities that include incremental generation and storage capacity likely to advance from the
interconnection queue, using historical success rates to estimate which projects could reasonably
reach commercial operation by 2029.

The Commission should clarify how customer load shed is defined and counted when applying the
magnitude criterion as the threshold is only meaningful if it reflects actual customer-facing outages

                                                21
 rather than internal operational curtailments. Large flexible load (LFL) curtailments under SB 6
should not be counted toward the 13,988 MW (2026) or 14,509 MW (2029) magnitude thresholds,
because these curtailments occur before rotating outages and materially change reserve-margin
outcomes. To ensure the magnitude criterion accurately reflects reliability risks for the broader
customer base, only rotating load shed affecting customers outside the LFL programs should be
included when determining whether the reliability standard is met.

ERCOT's proposed natural-gas and coal prices for 2026 and 2029 are materially understated relative
to forward-market expectations and Texas-specific structural drivers, risking underestimation of
scarcity conditions and misrepresentation of system behavior in the probabilistic assessment. More
accurate fuel-price inputs should be derived from recent forward-market data at relevant Texas hubs,
supplemented with updated delivered-coal cost information, and paired with weather-year daily
gas-price modeling to capture volatility during extreme events.

ERCOT's proposal to replace the fixed 85% weatherization-effectiveness assumption is appropriate
because a static value cannot reflect how outage risk increases under more extreme temperatures; a
temperature-dependent approach produces a more realistic representation of residual winter reliability
risk. As ERCOT gains additional empirical data from winter operations, the temperature-dependent
curves should be recalibrated to observed performance to ensure the model remains grounded in
real-world generator behavior.

Planned transmission outages are better addressed through ERCOT's operational planning and
outage-scheduling processes or in future targeted studies once the core reliability-assessment
framework is fully established and validated.

ERCOT should provide greater transparency into Energy Storage Resource modeling specifically
storage durations, cycling limits, and round-trip efficiency because these parameters materially
influence how storage contributes to reliability outcomes and are necessary for stakeholders to
interpret SERVM results accurately.
